title: M16 four-player host workload comparison
method: Same current executable, game library, renderer, baked-light fixture and camera positions in both runs; only the M16 package assets differ.
All four players hold their M16 at hip. Aim and firing captures occur after timing collection.
Runs are sequential. Blender and other task renders had completed.
Counters are summed across all four viewports per display frame. 360 samples remain after dropping the first 120 frames.
interpretation: Model triangles and client vertex submission bytes decreased with the same draw count and world triangle count.
Median whole-display completion time remained near the 120 FPS frame cap. This does not establish a meaningful whole-game FPS gain.
CPU-side screen work was lower in this host sample, but a single sequential software-renderer pair is not a Raspberry Pi performance forecast.

Pose interpolation work increased in this sample: 1580 to 2350 vertices, with eight to six pose-cache hits. The pattern is consistent with two distinct idle pose keys instead of one; actor pose timing was not synchronized. It is not evidence for a measured pose CPU reduction.
Resident buffer totals include the world and all registered models. The viewmodel xyz calculation isolates the M16 static position buffer. Per-frame static uploads remained zero after registration.

The M16 first-person muzzle flash follows the ADS translation; existing recoil, raise and bob still make its camera-basis anchor an approximation, not an exact attachment to the final procedural barrel pose.

viewmodel_static_xyz.calculation: One resident xyz buffer, three float32 components per render vertex; shared across four view draws.
